items.title: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer
items.original_title: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer
items.rss_title: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer
items.rss_description: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer Claims ITL Editorial Team Tue, 10/06/2026 - 11:19 Chief claims officers must transform their departments into AI-native ground-truth engines or risk becoming the bottleneck in enterprise transformation. October 7, 2026 Image For decades, the mandate of the chief claims cfficer was relatively clear: build a strong organization to investigate claims, control costs, manage litigation, negotiate settlements, and deliver fair outcomes. That mandate is no longer sufficient. The 2027 chief claims officer has a much bigger job: build the insurer's ground-truth engine—an AI-native operation that produces superior outcomes, industrializes negotiation excellence, and converts what claims learns into intelligence for the entire enterprise. This is not simply about using AI to make legacy claims processes more efficient. AI is turning insurance into an information business—and the most important ground truth in that business is generated in claims. Claims reveal what actually happened to the risks the insurer underwrote, what drove the loss, and what ultimately determined its economic outcome. To compete in an AI world, insurers will need to capture that ground truth, make it machine-readable, and use it to improve underwriting, pricing, reserving, and portfolio management. That puts claims—and the chief claims officer—on the front line of this unprecedented transformation. A new competitive environment Claims officers in traditional claims organizations face urgent and pressing competition from two sources at once. On one side is an increasingly industrialized plaintiff bar. On the other side is a new generation of AI-native insurers, poised to move forward. On the first side, consider Morgan & Morgan. The personal-injury giant says it has invested roughly $300 million in technology and AI and plans at least $1 billion more over the next decade. Its proprietary MX2 platform supports medical-record extraction, case research, document generation, demand letters, and trial preparation, while Injury.com digitally acquires and qualifies potential claims. Private equity is adding fuel, investing in personal-injury platforms to scale technology, analytics, marketing and standardized operations. The plaintiff bar is turning claim development and negotiation from individual craftsmanship into an industrial system. On the second side, a new generation of AI-native insurers is being built without decades of legacy technology, workflows and organizational baggage. Companies such as Corgi are attempting to build insurance businesses from inception around modern data architectures, AI agents and technology-speed iteration. McKinsey has warned that AI-native insurance businesses can increasingly build and refine products in weeks while incumbents remain calibrated to annual planning cycles and multi-year transformations. Legacy insurers are being squeezed from both directions: out-innovated by the plaintiff bar in the contest over outcomes and potentially out-architected by AI-native insurers in the contest over how insurance itself operates. Claims sits directly in the middle. That changes the requirements of its leader. 1. Level the playing field with the plaintiff bar The plaintiff bar has largely approached AI as a weapon for improving economic outcomes. Carriers have largely approached it as a tool for workflow efficiency. AI-powered demand packages are working. Carriers are only beginning to experiment seriously with the corresponding AI-powered offer package. Meanwhile, sophisticated plaintiff organizations are accumulating data, developing proprietary AI and attracting enormous capital. The plaintiff bar is both the threat and the proof point. They are investing their own money—and increasing institutional capital—because better case development, persuasion, and negotiation improve their economics. The CCO must build institutional capabilities that can match increasingly industrialized counterparties. 2. Institutionalize negotiation excellence Most carriers have some excellent negotiators. That is no longer enough. If negotiation materially affects indemnity outcomes, it cannot remain an individual skill distributed unevenly across thousands of claims professionals. The organization should know who its elite negotiators are, why they outperform and how those behaviors can be replicated. Carriers that cannot identify, measure and reproduce negotiation excellence do not really possess a negotiation capability. They possess individual negotiators. The CCO must turn individual excellence into measurable institutional capability. 3. Stop putting AI band-aids on pre-AI claims operations Many carriers can produce an impressive list of AI-centric projects: summarize a file, extract information, draft correspondence, analyze a demand, route work, search notes, or give adjusters Copilot. Those applications can create real value. But old process plus an AI tool means slightly better old process. McKinsey has warned about layering new technology onto legacy insurance operating models. BCG similarly distinguishes between deploying AI into existing processes and reshaping workflows around AI. The CCO must redesign the operating model, not merely automate the existing one. 4. Build machine-first claims The traditional claim file was built primarily for humans. Documents, notes, emails, medical records, and litigation materials accumulate while experienced professionals gradually construct an understanding of what happened. In an AI-native operation, every claim should progressively become a machine-readable representation of the claim—the people, events, evidence, injuries, allegations, relationships, negotiations and outcomes. That structured claim becomes the substrate on which specialized AI agents can continuously reason. Instead of occasionally asking AI to summarize a file, machines continuously read, structure, monitor, compare, detect, and prepare. The CCO must make claims machine-readable while elevating, not diminishing, human judgment and action. 5. Build and lead a hybrid workforce The future claim officer will have two kinds of capacity at their disposal: human expertise and machine intelligence. AI agents will increasingly read, structure, monitor, research, compare, detect, analyze and prepare. Humans will increasingly concentrate on judgment, investigation, strategy, creativity, empathy, supervision, accountability and negotiation. That will make exceptional claims professionals more important, not less. Imagine an elite negotiator supported by agents that continuously understand the evidence, medical history, venue, plaintiff counsel, negotiation history, and comparable outcomes. The machine handles much of the cognitive preparation. The human concentrates on what exceptional humans do best: think, strategize, persuade, read the counterparty, exercise judgment, and negotiate. The CCO must become the architect of human and machine capacity—designing how each works together to produce better outcomes. 6. Make every negotiation a learning event A sophisticated plaintiff demand should eventually meet an equally sophisticated carrier response. But the bigger opportunity comes afterward. Every demand, analysis, strategy, offer, response, counteroffer, and outcome must become institutional knowledge in the same way that the plaintiff bar is institutionalizing these events. Which plaintiff firms consistently outperform? Which strategies work against them? Which facts change settlement value? Which negotiators outperform expectations? Where does the organization systematically overpay? Every negotiation should make the next negotiation smarter. The CCO must ensure every claim and negotiation makes the organization smarter. 7. Elevate claims into the insurer's ground-truth engine This is where the transformation extends beyond claims. Underwriting begins with hypotheses about risk. Pricing quantifies them. Reserving updates them. Claims discovers what was actually true. Claims learns what caused the loss, how injuries developed, what evidence mattered, how attorneys behaved, which defenses and negotiation strategies worked, and what the risk ultimately cost. Yet much of that knowledge remains trapped in PDFs, notes, litigation files and the heads of experienced claims professionals. Claims should continuously produce structured intelligence that flows into underwriting, pricing, reserving, risk, reinsurance and portfolio management. The claim is no longer simply something to resolve and close. It is one of the insurer's richest proprietary information assets. The CCO must turn claims knowledge into enterprise intelligence—making the claims organization the feedback loop that allows the entire enterprise to learn. 8. Don't let claims become the transformation bottleneck This may be the requirement that matters most to the rest of the C-suite. A legacy insurer can modernize distribution, underwriting, pricing and portfolio management. But if its richest source of ground truth remains trapped inside a document-centric, human-first claims operation moving through multi-year transformation cycles, the rest of the enterprise eventually hits a wall. AI-native competitors do not have to unwind decades of organizational architecture before redesigning how humans, machines and data work together. Incumbents do. That makes speed itself a competitive capability. The modern CCO must protect the integrity of a massive, consequential operation while simultaneously making it capable of continuous change. The plaintiff bar is moving at technology speed. AI-native competitors are being built for technology speed. Claims cannot continue moving at insurance speed. The CCO must ensure claims leads rather than constrains the insurer's AI transformation. The mandate has changed None of these requirements eliminates the traditional responsibilities of the CCO. Claims still must be handled fairly; customers, regulatory obligations, litigation, reserves and operational discipline still matter. But those responsibilities are increasingly table stakes. Sophisticated plaintiff organizations are industrializing the pursuit of settlement dollars while AI-native insurers are being architected as technology-speed information businesses. Between them sits a claims organization that, at many incumbents, was designed for another era. That creates both a threat and an extraordinary opportunity. Carriers that generate that ground truth better, negotiate from it more effectively, make it machine-readable and distribute it throughout the enterprise will possess something more valuable than a more efficient claims department. They will possess a continuously learning insurance enterprise. As chief claims officers enter 2027, the question is no longer whether their departments will use more AI. It is whether they can transform their departments into a competitive advantage rather than the bottleneck preventing the enterprise from changing with it. Taylor Smith John Burge

items.rss_description: Gen Z Drives Insurance Claims Transformation Customer Experience ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/14/2026 - 13:12 Gen Z's demand for instant digital experiences is forcing insurers to modernize claims payments or risk losing policyholders. October 15, 2026 Image As digital natives who've grown up tethered to smartphones and social media, the Gen Z population's effect on today's consumer trends is well documented . Young shoppers' demands for instant gratification in consumer transactions have ushered in an era of in-app shopping, next-day shipping, and fast, friction-free digital payment options. Gen Z's influence is extending to the insurance claims process, as well. More and more, Gen Z's preferences are pushing the industry to uplevel its claims experience – to make it faster, more convenient, more tied to mobile, and more transparent to the policyholder. InvoiceCloud's 2026 Claims Experience survey of 1,000 U.S. policyholders shows Gen Z is nearly twice as likely as the overall population to prefer a digital wallet for claims payments (13% versus 7%). Recent research shines a light on policyholders' discontent with what they identify as their biggest deal breaker: an unacceptably slow process for paying claims. The InvoiceCloud survey found that only 9% of policyholders received their claims payment within two days. Meanwhile, a quarter of respondents say it took more than a week to receive their claims payout, while an unfortunate 13% waited "several weeks" to get these urgent funds. This could cause ripple effects. In a 2022 report, " Transforming claims and underwriting with AI ", Accenture estimated that poor claims experiences could put up to $170 billion in global insurance premiums at risk through 2027. The InvoiceCloud survey shows how these risks could materialize. At least 75% of policyholders surveyed say they would consider switching carriers after a single negative claims experience. That's a high percentage in any field, but it's particularly high in personal-lines P&C, where switching providers is often easier than it is in commercial, E&S, or other specialty markets. Improving the claims process How do insurance carriers improve the claims process? Our research found that speed and transparency matter most of all to policyholders. When asked directly, 30% named a faster claims payment after approval as the single change they want most, more than any other option, while 22% preferred clearer status communication. Gen Z echoes that second point: 24% named clearer, more consistent communication about payment status as the one change they would make, on par with the 21% who named faster payment. Another issue: Many carriers have modernized inbound premium payments, but outbound disbursements still rely on paper checks and manual processing. Paper checks create fraud risk, delivery problems, and extra work for commissions and return premiums. The next generation of policyholders is demanding two changes to this payment structure. They prefer a shift to digital, and they want choices. Digital disbursement platforms can support a wide variety of options including ACH/direct deposit, debit cards, virtual cards, and digital wallets. Direct deposit to a bank account is policyholders' favorite payout, preferred by 52% of respondents, more than all other options combined. Printed checks still account for 19%, likely reflecting legacy carrier processes rather than genuine preference. The gap between generations is wide: 32% of Baby Boomers prefer a printed check, compared with just 9% of Gen Z. If slow payouts can lead to defections, digital insurance payments can operate as a retention tool. Insurance carriers can do this by ensuring this critical touchpoint becomes an easy experience end-to-end, from allowing policyholders to self-serve through digital premium payments, paperless billing, and automatic payments, to instant disbursements delivered however policyholders prefer to receive funds. Real-time digital disbursements are funds sent electronically and received quickly, without a paper check in the middle. For insurance carriers, this means agent commissions and return premiums move through digital payment processing solutions rather than the mail. More importantly, it means getting funds into policyholders' hands fast, when it matters the most. Raising expectations As younger policyholders account for a larger share of the insurance market, experiences they've grown accustomed to in other walks of life will increasingly become expectations for insurance as well. For many, this translates to being able to complete more transactions on smartphones. Digital payments enable customers to choose a payment method from their phone, receive payment notifications, track payment status, access transaction details, and receive funds directly into an eligible account or wallet. That matters most to the youngest policyholders. When asked for the easiest way to access funds in an emergency, 19% of Gen Z chose a mobile wallet, compared with 5% of Baby Boomers, while only 9% would withdraw cash at a bank, compared with 34% of Baby Boomers. Gen Z's imprint on insurance claims is becoming more pronounced. Today's policyholders want to have insurance claims processed and paid out faster. But they want more. They want the entire journey – culminating in how and when they get paid – to feel as immediate and seamless as any other digital financial transaction. Ray Walsh

items.title: Why Are Insurance Jobs Disappearing?
items.original_title: Why Are Insurance Jobs Disappearing?
items.rss_title: Why Are Insurance Jobs Disappearing?
items.rss_description: Why Are Insurance Jobs Disappearing? PaulCarroll Mon, 10/05/2026 - 17:40 The employment report for September in the U.S. showed a loss of 7,000 jobs in financial services. Insurance, alone, has now lost 90,000 jobs since May 2025. What's going on? I have a theory, and it's not about artificial intelligence. If I'm right, hiring in insurance will stay in the doldrums for a while. Let's have a look. As Insurance Business reports , the industry still employs a massive 2.9 million people in the U.S., but claims jobs are down a hefty 21% over the past year, while life and health is off 4%, P&C down 1.7%, and agents and brokers down 1.1%. The losses are accelerating: The article says, " Insurers lost about 1,900 jobs a month on average in 2025 and roughly 6,900 a month so far in 2026." A thorough analysis in Barron's mostly attributes the job losses to cost-cutting under pressure. Barron's notes that the surge in rates following the COVID disruption has slowed. In addition, government subsidies for healthcare have been cut even as claims costs keep increasing. In the face of pressure on both premiums and expenses, insurers have had to become more efficient, Barron's says. It does say AI has played a role by automating tasks but doesn't treat that as a huge issue just yet (and I've been arguing for months that the fears of job losses to AI are overstated). You could also add the effects of the "silver tsunami" -- the oft-quoted projection by the Bureau of Labor Statistics in 2021 that 400,000 insurance professionals would retire by the end of 2026. Unemployment in insurance remains well below that for the economy writ large -- 3.1%, vs. 4.2% -- so some of the job losses may simply be that companies haven't yet been able to fill the positions left by retirements. But I think there's an overarching issue that gets short shrift if you spend too much time in the details. My Theory My theory boils down to uncertainty. I think economic and geopolitical uncertainty are holding back the economy, in general, and the insurance industry, in particular. And I don't see the uncertainty subsiding any time soon. Tariffs have not only raised costs but, because of their on-again, off-again nature, have slowed investment and the sort of adaptation of supply chains that would ordinarily happen if, say, Canadian lumber suddenly became 50% more expensive. Why spend a lot of money and time if prices might return to normal shortly, whether because of a court ruling against tariffs, because Democrats win control of Congress and assert its power, or simply because President Trump changed his mind? Now add the uncertainty from the war on Iran. Even though oil flows out of the Middle East are improving, Iran retains the capability to attack tankers, to blow up one of the major pipelines being used to skirt the Strait of Hormuz, or to do more damage to the diesel refineries in the region, whose loss has contributed so much to the soaring prices for the crucial fuel. While Trump has repeatedly told us that Iran wants to make a deal and that prices for oil will soon plummet, some of us are old enough to remember how the Iranian zealots acted after taking 66 American hostages in 1979. Angry at President Carter, they didn't release the hostages until minutes after Ronald Reagan became president in January 1981. Who's to say the Iranian theocrats won't treat Trump the way their predecessors treated Carter, declining to make a deal until he leaves office? What is now looking like a blue wave in next month's midterm elections might relieve some of the uncertainty about tariffs, perhaps even leading to serious settlement talks with Iran, but a loss of control by Trump would surely lead to at least a burst of chaos -- perhaps even a sustained stretch. The Democrats are itching to go after him, and he would surely return fire with every one of the many assets at his disposal. The current uncertainty and the prospects that it will continue will create headwinds for the economy, which insurance, especially P&C, tracks closely. The problem will be even worse than normal, I believe, because the effects will hit personal lines so hard. Replacement costs for cars have surged in recent years because of supply chain disruptions, and they will likely stay in flux. Insurers will also have to deal with possibly significant changes in driver behavior if gasoline and diesel prices stay so high -- or go even higher. Costs for home repairs have likewise soared, and uncertainty will tend to keep them high. Meanwhile, the general uncertainty about the economy has fueled inflation, leading the Fed to raise rates for the first time in years and to signal that it may raise rates again soon. A result has been 7% mortgages that have pretty much crushed the housing sector. The reduction in construction means fewer homes to insure, and the stagnant resale market limits the opportunities to poach customers as homes change hands. The result will, I believe, be unrelenting pressure on revenue and costs at a time when customers are exhausted from all the post-COVID rate increases. I hope I'm wrong, but it's hard to see a lot of hiring in that sort of environment. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll The latest jobs report for the U.S. highlighted a surprising decline in employment in insurance. I have a theory about the reason -- and it's not AI. The current uncertainty and the prospects that it will continue will create headwinds for the economy, which insurance, especially P&C, tracks closely. The problem will be even worse than normal, I believe, because the effects will hit personal lines so hard. Replacement costs for cars have surged in recent years because of supply chain disruptions, and they will likely stay in flux. Insurers will also have to deal with possibly significant changes in driver behavior if gasoline and diesel prices stay so high -- or go even higher. Costs for home repairs have likewise soared, and uncertainty will tend to keep them high. Meanwhile, the general uncertainty about the economy has fueled inflation, leading the Fed to raise rates for the first time in years and to signal that it may raise rates again soon. A result has been 7% mortgages that have pretty much crushed the housing sector. The reduction in construction means fewer homes to insure, and the stagnant resale market limits the opportunities to poach customers as homes change hands. The result will, I believe, be unrelenting pressure on revenue and costs at a time when customers are exhausted from all the post-COVID rate increases. I hope I'm wrong, but it's hard to see a lot of hiring in that sort of environment. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll The latest jobs report for the U.S. highlighted a surprising decline in employment in insurance. I have a theory about the reason -- and it's not AI. items.extracted_text: Lloyd's issues guidance and expectations for broker-originated reinsurance structures - Artemis.bm Lloyd's issues guidance and expectations for broker-originated reinsurance structures - Artemis.bm Lloyd’s issues guidance and expectations for broker-originated reinsurance structures 16th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans As industry focus grows on designing efficient structures to enable capital to connect with reinsurance risk, Lloyd’s has issued guidance on its expectations for any broker-originated reinsurance structures, which is a strategy that Lloyd’s itself believes is likely to see increasing demand. The issue of this guidance note from Lloyd’s comes on the heels of the high-profile news around Aon’s partnership with Blackstone on the vehicle widely said to be codenamed Cortina. That strategy sees Aon looking to bring Blackstone into Lloyd’s, to support a share of the business it brokers in the market, which represents another signal of capital market and asset manager appetite to gain access to broadly diversified insurance and reinsurance market returns. Lloyd’s framework for broker-originated reinsurance structures provides market guidance as to the approach, its expectations and what the approval requirements will be for broker-originated reinsurance structures. The Aon – Blackstone news raised many questions, so this appears to be at least in part a response to that, to place some clarity around what Lloyd’s will tolerate and expect from those seeking to replicate, or design different structures to achieve similar outcomes (the outcomes being new capital entrants backing meaningful portfolios of risk underwritten there). Third-party capital’s appetite to access returns from the reinsurance market in general and business from Lloyd’s has risen fast in the last couple of years. At the same time, new structures and strategies are making it possible to bring capital market participants more deeply into the Lloyd’s market, in support of syndicates, so-called ReShares and broker facilities. In addition, the London Bridge structures have also provided more efficient mechanisms for routing third-party capital into the market’s underwriting workflow. Lloyd’s explained in a market bulletin issued by Rachel Turk, Chief of Performance and Strategy, “The growth of broker facilities and third-party capital solutions has created an emerging opportunity for broker-led reinsurance portfolios supported by external capital. We expect demand for these structures to increase. “We have today issued a clear framework for how these structures are overseen at Lloyd’s that will take effect from 1st January 2027. The framework is transparent, principles-based, and provides the market with clarity on Lloyd’s appetite, expectations and guardrails for such structures. “The new framework seeks to support innovation and growth while maintaining underwriting discipline and protecting the Central Fund. It is anchored around Lloyd’s cross-cycle 95% net combined operating ratio target and establishes clear requirements relating to market concentration, ownership and capital, governance, managing agent capabilities, underwriting guardrails, portfolio oversight and eligibility criteria. “Consistent with Lloyd’s broader approach, broker-originated reinsurance structures are subject to the standard new entrant approval process and ongoing oversight arrangements.” Facilities have existed at Lloyd’s for many years, including broker run facility structures. But, in the past these have tended to have multiple markets backing them, largely traditional insurance and reinsurance players. Where as now, we see asset managers and capital markets players having facilities-of-one, of sorts, as they seek to derive exposure to an index, or index of a sub-set of the Lloyd’s markets underwriting business and returns. As a strategy, it makes perfect sense, in delivering large-scale access to a broad and diversified swathe of risk. But for Lloyd’s, there is the rest of the market and its participants to consider, hence the issuance of guidelines to help the market understand what will be allowed and tolerated. Lloyd’s has explained some of the features of its framework for broker-originated reinsurance structures in the market. Any such venture will need to show its alignment with Lloyd’s cross-cycle 95% net combined operating ratio target, while they will initially be curtailed to a market-wide risk appetite of up to 10% of an individual broker’s treaty portfolio that can be placed into these structures. In addition, Lloyd’s said that brokers cannot own or capitalise these reinsurance structures themselves. Of course, that would be a step too far over the boundary between broker and underwriter. There has to be a minimum capital participation requirement from the member aligned to the managing agent of 19.99%, while at least 25% of capacity must be provided by the lead reinsurers, with the panel agreed by the managing agent. Some business is considered out of scope for broker-originated reinsurance structures in Lloyd’s, including hybrid fronting carriers, MGUs and legacy providers, captive involvement needs a prior submit arrangement and there can be no exposure to Cyber war “type 4” language. Interestingly, Lloyd’s also seems to want to see a commitment from those participating as cedents, saying, “Once the participation cede has been determined as part of the overall proposition, cedents must cede either all of their eligible portfolio with the respective broker to the structure, or none of it.” While the managing agent must be sophisticated enough, in terms of reinsurance analysis and pricing, to challenge the assumptions provided by the broker. Reporting and oversight will be key, with regular engagement with Lloyd’s and data sharing, as well as agreed guardrails needing to be in place that the capital provider and managing agent must contractually agree on. Importantly, Lloyd’s does not want these structures running unfettered, saying, “If indexation of at least 70% has not been reached by year 3 of the structure, Lloyd’s and the managing agent will agree next steps which can include winding up the structure.” Annual plans and any mid-year changes will need to be approved, as they are for other more traditional Lloyd’s underwriting structures. While standard new entrant capital allocation rules and timings will apply. Finally and perhaps the most important guideline, efficiencies generated by the broker-originated reinsurance strategy must find their way back to the protection buyers. Lloyd’s will expect the cedent to share in the efficiencies generated by the structure (both operational and capital) through the mechanism of a client dividend, the market explained. Lloyd’s stated, “The framework applies to all broker-originated reinsurance structures seeking approval to operate within Lloyd’s and should be considered alongside the standard new entrant approval process.” Alternative, third-party and capital markets investors are extremely interested in efficient ways to gain access to insurance and reinsurance risks at this time and over recent years Lloyd’s has itself shown that it is increasingly open to seeing new capital enter the market in more efficient ways. It’s important to have some guidelines around it, so it’s good to see the market responding and issuing this bulletin. However, it does raise one question. How many similar strategies of meaningful scale, backed by large capital market players (the Blackstone types), could and should Lloyd’s allow, without risking upsetting the broader market’s sentiment and equilibrium? Of course, if efficient capital can be put to work to bring much more underwriting business into Lloyd’s that is a good thing, as long as discipline and prudence are observed. But we all know what too much capital can do and there is a perhaps-challenging balancing-act to be followed, to keep the established market participants on-side as Lloyd’s itself evolves and broker’s increasingly marshal capital more directly to risk. items.title: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why?
items.original_title: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why?
items.rss_title: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why?
items.rss_description: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why? PaulCarroll Mon, 10/12/2026 - 17:45 The recent report that auto thefts fell 21% in the U.S. in the first half of the year reminds me of a friend's carjacking some 30 years ago — surely the shortest in history. My overeducated friend, with degrees from Brown and the Sorbonne, had just added a certification as an auto mechanic and liked cars that required constant tinkering. While driving near his home in Washington, DC, one afternoon, he stopped at a stop sign, and a pedestrian motioned to him that he had a question. Tim rolled down his window, and the man shoved a gun in his face, ordering him out of the car. The man got in, engaged the clutch and drove... two feet. He tried again, but the car stalled after two more feet. He tried a third time. A fourth. He hadn't even made it halfway into the intersection before he jumped out, threw the keys at Tim's chest and ran off. I'd never thought of having a diseased clutch as an anti-theft device but have watched with interest over the years as actual devices have continually improved. They've now gotten to the point that, combined with other factors, thefts fell 17% in 2024, tumbled 23% last year, to the lowest levels in decades, and are way down again this year. The good news for insurers is likely to continue, too. Let's have a look. Some of my optimism stems simply from the steady modernization of the car fleet. Even though soaring prices for cars have encouraged people to hold on to cars longer than in the past, older, more vulnerable cars are steadily being retired, and that trend will continue. In the face of public pressure, companies whose cars were most likely to be stolen have also issued software patches and other updates — as a result, the percentage of car thefts of Kias and Hyundais fell to 14% of the total last year, from 16% in 2024 and 21% in 2023, even as the total of thefts dropped precipitously. Meanwhile, the supply chain has sorted itself out post-COVID, so thieves can't rack up the sorts of profits they did from stealing scarce parts in recent years. The U.S. war on Iran may unsettle the supply chain again, including by pushing sales of electric vehicles during a time of high gasoline prices, but the effects have been muted so far, and I suspect they'll remain so. Law enforcement has stepped up efforts to prevent all sorts of crimes, and car thefts are a visible target at just about all levels of policing. I'm not sure how much more severe enforcement can become, but, especially in a fraught political environment, I don't see that anyone will relax. Potentially the most important — but fraught — factor that will determine how much car thefts keep falling relates to surveillance technology. Flock has built a massive business by installing cameras on roads nationwide that take pictures of license plates and respond to, among other things, alerts from police departments about stolen vehicles. There are lots of efforts to also figure out how to knit together all the images being gathered by dashcams, which are currently in about one in 10 vehicles in the U.S. and which are being adopted quickly. Combining all those feeds could provide real-time intelligence for police departments, making it far easier to catch thieves and creating a massive disincentive for them to steal cars in the first place. But.... We've also seen how surveillance can be abused, as I wrote in August . Flock faces a scandal because dozens of police officers used its technology to stalk current and former romantic partners, and the temptation to use surveillance illicitly will only increase as the technology becomes more powerful. My gut tells me that it will take time, perhaps years, to sort through all the tensions between law enforcement and privacy but that we'll eventually get to the point where some severely circumscribed uses of license plate readers will take another cut out of auto thefts. The privacy issue is one we've mostly navigated with Ring cameras and surveillance cameras on building, so there's a blueprint for progress The bad guys are always innovating, just as the good guys are, but I think the favorable glide path for car thefts should continue. Cheers, Paul P.S. My other bizarro car theft story, this one involving a nephew and an odd situation for the adjuster: While my nephew was visiting DC last year, his Hyundai was stolen off the street by four kids — who drove the car right past him as he was talking with the police officer who responded to his report of the crime. They took the car on joy rides for a few days — as evidenced by the thousands of dollars of traffic violations they ran up in DC and Maryland — then used it in a drug deal that went bad. The car wound up full of bullet holes, and a friend of the kids was shot. Panicking, the kids put the badly wounded girl in the trunk of the car and dumped her in front of her high school. These young geniuses then abandoned the car and tried to run off but were promptly apprehended by school security. (The girl healed fine.) The insurance issue was that the adjuster couldn't look at the car because it was in police custody as a crime scene. So my nephew's insurer kept him in a rental car for weeks until it finally satisfied itself that the car was a total loss and wrote him a check for a new one. My nephew spent weeks unwinding the traffic tickets. He actually had to drive to Baltimore from Philadelphia to appear in court and provide evidence that he couldn't have been at the wheel for the moving violations because he wasn't in Maryland when they occurred. Image Paul Carroll Car thefts in the U.S. tumbled to their lowest levels in decades in 2025, and are down a further 21% this year. The trend is likely to continue, too. Flock faces a scandal because dozens of police officers used its technology to stalk current and former romantic partners, and the temptation to use surveillance illicitly will only increase as the technology becomes more powerful. My gut tells me that it will take time, perhaps years, to sort through all the tensions between law enforcement and privacy but that we'll eventually get to the point where some severely circumscribed uses of license plate readers will take another cut out of auto thefts. The privacy issue is one we've mostly navigated with Ring cameras and surveillance cameras on building, so there's a blueprint for progress The bad guys are always innovating, just as the good guys are, but I think the favorable glide path for car thefts should continue. Cheers, Paul P.S. My other bizarro car theft story, this one involving a nephew and an odd situation for the adjuster: While my nephew was visiting DC last year, his Hyundai was stolen off the street by four kids — who drove the car right past him as he was talking with the police officer who responded to his report of the crime. They took the car on joy rides for a few days — as evidenced by the thousands of dollars of traffic violations they ran up in DC and Maryland — then used it in a drug deal that went bad. The car wound up full of bullet holes, and a friend of the kids was shot. Panicking, the kids put the badly wounded girl in the trunk of the car and dumped her in front of her high school. These young geniuses then abandoned the car and tried to run off but were promptly apprehended by school security. (The girl healed fine.) The insurance issue was that the adjuster couldn't look at the car because it was in police custody as a crime scene. So my nephew's insurer kept him in a rental car for weeks until it finally satisfied itself that the car was a total loss and wrote him a check for a new one. My nephew spent weeks unwinding the traffic tickets. He actually had to drive to Baltimore from Philadelphia to appear in court and provide evidence that he couldn't have been at the wheel for the moving violations because he wasn't in Maryland when they occurred. Image Paul Carroll Car thefts in the U.S. tumbled to their lowest levels in decades in 2025, and are down a further 21% this year. The trend is likely to continue, too. items.rss_description: TESTING focus newsletter grant Thu, 10/01/2026 - 15:37 some summary here October 1, 2026 View this email in your browser | Forward to a colleague ITL FOCUS is a monthly initiative featuring topics related to innovation in risk management and insurance. This month, we're focusing on IT Ops: Change Management FROM THE EDITOR Some two decades into the insurance industry's digital transformation, companies have spent hundreds of billions of dollars on new core systems, cloud migrations, digital portals, and AI tools — but the technology was rarely the hardest part. The hardest part was the people. The people part has long been treated as a supporting act in large technology transformations. But as the pace and complexity of transformation accelerates, that approach is showing its limits. Employees nod along, say they're using the new system, and then quietly find workarounds. Leadership mandates adoption from the top while alignment quietly fractures below. Organizations sprint to the go-live date and then discover that the real work hadn't started yet. Samit Bhandari has watched this pattern play out across the P&C insurance industry for 20 years as a partner at PwC. He's worked with carriers of all sizes through core system replacements, AI rollouts, and full-scale digital transformations — and has seen where these programs succeed and where they quietly go off the rails. He acknowledges there has been improvement—he says the assumption that most large technology programs fail is increasingly out of date. But he says organizations keep making a lot of the same, old mistakes, including the tendency to underinvest in what happens after a go-live, to confuse executive messaging with genuine alignment, and to treat transformation as a one-time event rather than a continuous process. Read the full interview to find out what red flags signal a change management program in trouble, why smaller carriers are often better at transformation than their larger counterparts, and what Bhandari thinks the industry has stopped doing that it should start doing again. continue reading > Reducing the Risk in Change Management Paul Carroll There's often a disconnect in technology adoption that goes unnoticed in business. A leader might mandate the use of AI, and employees will say they're using it—but are they really changing the way they do things, or are they just going through the motions to show compliance? How do you get people on the same page in a big technology transformation? Samit Bhandari First, just in terms of getting everyone on the same page, it's the fundamentals of what we've always said about getting stakeholders engaged—executive, top-down engagement early, right? The messaging from that level through various levels of the organization. And then just the strategic, tactical things—the change champion network and the communication early and often. When you bring in AI—we should be more nimble. read the full interview > MORE ON CHANGE MANAGEMENT Change Management Is Changing by Melissa Palmer Change management can no longer be viewed as a one-time project discipline. It must become an organizational capability. Read More How to Put People First in Your AI Rollout by Tracey Brown "We made a deliberate decision to treat employee confidence as the primary KPI of our AI transformation." items.extracted_text: Swiss Re: Non-Economic Factors Drive Half of UK Liability Claims Growth Article 0 Comments Non-economic factors have accounted for roughly half of liability claims growth in the U.K. in the last six years, according to a new report. The report from Swiss Re Institute, High U.K. Liability Claims Growth Could Increase Without Balanced Reforms, shows non-economic factors added 5 to 6 percentage points to liability claims growth in 2024. That’s the fifth straight year of elevated liability excess inflation. Related: Business Interruption Claims Are Approaching $1M Average Non-economic drivers include changes in laws and legal procedures, litigation funding and claimant behavior. The U.K. has experienced faster growth in liability excess inflation than some other European markets. The report also identifies several pending legal and regulatory reforms that could further increase liability claims costs, including the U.K.’s planned reversal of a 2023 court ruling, R (PACCAR Inc) v. Competition Appeal Tribunal , which made certain litigation funding agreements unenforceable. The government committed to reversing the ruling through legislation, and the authors of the report expect litigation activity to increase if the ruling is reversed. Related: Report: Property Claims Face Delays, Are Growing More Complex Another proposed change involves expanding collective legal actions beyond competition law. A review of consumer class action rules is considering whether to allow claimants to be automatically included in lawsuits unless they opt out, which the report’s authors say could increase the number of claimants and make litigation funding more financially attractive. The report also cites an economic analysis estimating that litigation funded by third parties and involving collective redress could generate £11.9 billion ($15.7 billion) in costs and compensation for U.K. businesses. The report identifies litigation funding transparency, claimant control over settlement decisions and alternative dispute resolution as potential safeguards against further claims inflation. The institute’s analysis uses a liability excess inflation index covering domestically located U.K. risks. Was this article valuable? Yes No Here are more articles you may enjoy. items.title: Comp benefits in school bus driver’s fatal crash upheld
items.original_title: Comp benefits in school bus driver’s fatal crash upheld
items.rss_title: Comp benefits in school bus driver’s fatal crash upheld
items.rss_description: A New York appeals court on Thursday upheld workers compensation and death benefits claims involving a school bus driver whose employer argued that an unrelated cardiac event caused his fatal crash.
items.extracted_text: Walter Greek, a driver for Dansville Central School District, was driving an empty bus into the district’s bus garage parking lot on April 5, 2022, when he lost control and struck a parked bus. He was found in cardiac arrest and remained comatose until his death five days later, according to Matter of Greek v. Dansville Central School District , decided by the Appellate Division, Third Department. Mr. Greek had been treated for an irregular heartbeat and cardiomyopathy but had been cleared to safely operate a commercial vehicle. Following the crash, doctors diagnosed brain injuries from prolonged loss of circulation, along with kidney, lung and rib injuries. The self-insured district argued that a cardiac event unrelated to work caused Mr. Greek to lose consciousness and that resuscitation efforts caused his rib and lung injuries. His treating cardiologists testified, however, that chest trauma could have triggered the abnormal heart rhythm. One said it was impossible to determine with certainty whether the arrhythmia preceded the crash or resulted from it. The district’s medical reviewer acknowledged assuming that a cardiac event occurred first. The appeals court upheld the Workers’ Compensation Board’s finding that the injuries arose from the work-related accident or necessary treatment. It also upheld death benefits, citing a medical examiner’s testimony that crash injuries placed additional stress on Mr. Greek’s heart and contributed to his death. The court said that a work-related injury need only contribute to a worker’s death to support death benefits. The district also sought to end Mr. Greek’s injury claim because he died before it could be resolved. The court found that surveillance footage, medical records and an independent medical review allowed the district to contest the claim despite his death. items.extracted_text: Generali launching Lloyd's Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge, to enhance access to reinsurance capital - Artemis.bm Generali launching Lloyd's Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge, to enhance access to reinsurance capital - Artemis.bm Generali launching Lloyd’s Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge, to enhance access to reinsurance capital 16th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Global re/insurer Generali is the latest to enter the Lloyd’s market with what seems a sidecar-like syndicate as a way to enhance and make its reinsurance arrangements more efficient, while the announcements points to the potential for alternative and capital markets to be involved. Generali said today it is entering Lloyd’s with the launch of Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge, for which it has now received in-principle approval to begin underwriting operations on the Lloyd’s platform in 2027. The insurer said this move is “a significant step forward in the Group’s reinsurance strategy, enhancing access to diversified sources of risk capital while reinforcing long-term partnerships across the global reinsurance market.” Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge will assume a share of Generali’s outward reinsurance placements, across multiple lines of business. As such this seems the latest example of a sidecar-style syndicate at Lloyd’s for a major re/insurance group. In addition, Generali said that its entry to Lloyd’s brings “a distinctive diversification opportunity” given the insurer’s geographical footprint and type of ceded businesses. Generali’s outward reinsurance portfolio offers significant exposure to continental European risks, the company explained, which it sees as a complement to Lloyd’s more traditional global focus. It also provides a balanced mix of retail and middle market business access across multiple classes and territories. Franco Urlini, Group P&C & Reinsurance Officer of Generali, explained, “The launch of Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge marks an important milestone in the evolution of our reinsurance strategy under the “Lifetime Partner 27: Driving Excellence” plan, with the goal to optimise capital at Group level. By leveraging the Lloyd’s global platform, we can develop tailored and innovative risk transfer solutions while accessing new sources of capital to support the growth ambitions of our P&C portfolio. It is an extension of our strategy aimed at maintaining broad and diversified access to reinsurance and alternative capital markets while adding a further tool to the Group’s risk transfer capabilities.” Note Urlini’s mention of accessing “new sources of capital” while also citing Generali’s strategy to diversify sources using alternative capital markets. Dawn Miller, Chief Commercial Officer of Lloyd’s and CEO of Lloyd’s Americas, added, “Our ambition is to attract the leading global underwriters to Lloyd’s, so we are delighted to be welcoming Generali with the launch of Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge. This vehicle will open up deeper connections between insurance, reinsurance and capital markets, underscoring Lloyd’s role as the leading global marketplace for innovative risk transfer solutions.” Note there, that Miller mentioned that Generali’s syndicate will deepen connections to capital markets as well. The commentary suggests that there may be a plan to bring in capital market backers to the syndicate, as a result it’s also possible that Lloyd’s insurance-linked securities (ILS) structure might be used, the London Bridge 2 PCC vehicle. It’s important to add that at this stage, no clarity has been given as to the backers of Generali’s syndicate, whether there is outside capital in from the start, or the insurer is funding it, or how capital will be channelled. But, given the strategy of ceding a portion of its outwards reinsurance placement to the syndicate, it perhaps suggests there might be more direct participation from other capital providers. As we said though, that is not immediately made clear from the announcement. The use of the Lloyd’s platform to set up sidecar style reinsurance syndicates, to optimise and enhance reinsurance programmes and capital usage, is a growing trend, often involving the London Bridge platform. In the last year we’ve seen Blackstone partner with The Fidelis Partnership on Syndicate 2126 , while the same asset manager partnered with AIG on Syndicate 2479 , which was that insurer’s second such vehicle after the also Blackstone-partnered Syndicate 2478 . Apollo has been selected as the managing agent for this new syndicate. Reinsurance brokerage Howden Re, acted as Generali’s exclusive adviser on the transaction, working across Howden Re International, Howden Re Capital Solutions and Howden Capital Markets & Advisory. Massimo Reina, CEO, Howden Re International, said, “This transaction demonstrates the value of combining deep insurance sector expertise with a strong understanding of Lloyd’s capital. Working as one team across Howden, we have supported Generali in creating a tailored platform designed to broaden its strategic options and attract third-party support from across the Lloyd’s capital ecosystem. Interest in the opportunity reflects the continued appeal of the Lloyd’s market to a diverse range of capital providers.” Vijay Mavani, Managing Director, Howden Capital Solutions, added, “This transaction demonstrates the value of the integrated Howden platform, combining deep reinsurance expertise, capital solutions capabilities and a strong understanding of Lloyd’s capital. Working closely with Philipp Kusche and colleagues across Howden Capital Markets & Advisory, we have operated as one team to support Generali in creating a tailored platform designed to broaden its strategic options and facilitate access to capital from across the Lloyd’s ecosystem. The level of interest in the opportunity highlights the continued attractiveness of the Lloyd’s market to a diverse range of capital providers.” Also read from earlier today: Lloyd’s issues guidance and expectations for broker-originated reinsurance structures . items.extracted_text: Moody’s estimates insured losses from hurricane Isaias in $2.5bn to $4.5bn range - Artemis.bm Moody’s estimates insured losses from hurricane Isaias in $2.5bn to $4.5bn range - Artemis.bm Moody’s estimates insured losses from hurricane Isaias in $2.5bn to $4.5bn range 16th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Moody’s RMS Event Response has now provided an initial estimate of insurance industry losses from recent hurricane Isaias, placing them in a range between $2.5 billion and $4.5 billion. Moody’s said that its best estimate is $3.5 billion, as you might expect the mid-point of the range and that the estimate represents insured losses from wind, storm surge, and precipitation-induced flooding damages. Wind damage is the majority of the losses from hurricane Isaias, Moody’s explained, while storm surge, precipitation-induced inland flooding, and the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) losses are expected to be only around $250 million of the total. Moody’s estimate includes insured property damage and business interruption for residential, commercial, industrial, automobile, as well as watercraft lines of business, and it also accounts for sources of post-event loss amplification (PLA). We can compare Moody’s estimate to others, such as the most recent from Karen Clark & Company (KCC) that estimated the private insurance market loss from wind and storm surge associated with recent hurricane Isaias would be $3 billion . Verisk gave its initial industry insured loss estimate for Isaias recently, saying that onshore property losses from the storm could reach $2 billion . In addition, Euler ILS Partners, the specialist Swiss insurance-linked securities (ILS) investment manager, put an initial insurance industry loss estimate for recent hurricane Isaias in the range of $2 billion to $4 billion . Cotality (formerly CoreLogic), estimated that insured losses from wind and storm surge from hurricane Isaias will be in the $2 billion to $3 billion range, while Gallagher Re said industry losses will fall in the lower end of the low to mid-single-digit billions of dollars range and AM Best said insured loss estimates are expected to be in the low single digit range in billions of dollars. Moody’s estimate is one of the higher, but still all the estimates top-out at $4.5 billion in range terms, at which level hurricane Isaias is not expected to be a significant reinsurance event, aside from perhaps a few very low layers and any quota share reinsurance participations that are exposed. Jeff Waters, Director – North Atlantic Hurricane Models, Moody’s, commented: “Hurricane Isaias was yet another example of a storm that intensified quickly over the anomalously warm ocean waters in the Gulf, a region that usually sees higher hurricane activity during El Niño years. Thankfully, the storm encountered strong wind shear as it approached landfall, which disrupted its structure and weakened the wind field considerably. As a result, we expect the overall extent and severity of insured losses from this event to be manageable for the market.” Raj Vojjala, Managing Director – Modeling and Analytics, Moody’s, said, “Many exposures impacted by Hurricane Isaias were also impacted by recent storms like Hurricanes Sally and Zeta in 2020, and Helene in 2024, which led to widespread roof repairs and replacements. We expect these efforts to have improved the risk profile and structural resilience of the region’s building stock to hurricane winds, especially for an event like Isaias. items.extracted_text: SafePoint targets $250m Nature Coast Re 2026-2 cat bond, for broadest coverage yet - Artemis.bm SafePoint targets $250m Nature Coast Re 2026-2 cat bond, for broadest coverage yet - Artemis.bm SafePoint targets $250m Nature Coast Re 2026-2 cat bond, for broadest coverage yet 16th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans SafePoint Insurance Company is back in the catastrophe bond, with an initial target to secure $250 million of multi-year named storm reinsurance protection from capital market investors through a Nature Coast Re Ltd. (Series 2026-2) cat bond issuance, Artemis has learned. SafePoint Insurance Company is an expansive insurance platform and in this case the company is demonstrating its growth, by seeking named storm reinsurance across the widest range of US states of any cat bond it has sponsored before. In 2025 SafePoint sponsored two catastrophe bonds, securing $200 million of annual aggregate and industry-loss trigger based reinsurance from a Nature Coast Re 2025-1 deal in January and then in April adding $150 million of indemnity based reinsurance with a Nature Coast Re 2025-2 issuance. The insurer has already been to market in 2026 as well, having secured $250 million of indemnity named storm reinsurance from the Nature Coast Re Ltd. (Series 2026-1) issuance in February this year. Now, the company is back to sponsor what will become its sixth cat bond under the Nature Coast Re special purpose insurer, and its tenth cat bond sponsorship in total. Read about all of SafePoint’s cat bonds in our extensive Deal Directory. Nature Coast Re Ltd. is offering investors two tranches of Series 2026-2 catastrophe bond notes that will be sold to investors to provide the collateral to fully-support underlying reinsurance agreements. Like other recent cat bonds from the company, the reinsurance agreements will protect SafePoint Insurance Company itself and the two reciprocal exchanges it operates, the Louisiana focused Cajun Underwriters Reciprocal Exchange entity, and the Florida homeowner and business owner focused Manatee Insurance Exchange. As we said, this new cat bond is designed to cover the widest range of US states of any cat bond in SafePoint’s history, as the insurer continues to expand and grow into new locations and so secure broader reinsurance arrangements to protect its book. Both tranches of the Nature Coast Re 2026-2 cat bond issuance are designed to provide SafePoint and its reciprocal underwriting entities with a source of fully-collateralized reinsurance protection covering losses from named storms across the states of Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee and Texas. Both tranches of notes from this cat bond are structured to provide protection to SafePoint’s underwriting entities on an indemnity and per-occurrence trigger basis, while the reinsurance will run across a four-year period from December 1st, we are told. A currently $100 million tranche of Series 2026-2 Class AA notes are the less risky later, having an attachment point of $300 million, taking a share of losses up to exhaustion at $600 million, sources said, giving room for the issuance to be upsized from the initial target, should SafePoint elect to. The $100 million of Series 2026-2 Class AA notes that Nature Coast Re is offering come with an initial attachment probability of 0.86%, an initial base expected loss of 0.73% and are being offered to investors with price guidance in a range for a spread of between 4% and 4.75%, we understand. A currently $150 million tranche of Series 2026-2 Class A notes are more risky later, still having an attachment point of $300 million, but taking a share of losses up to exhaustion at $1.3 billion, sources said, again giving room for upsizing. The $150 million of Series 2026-2 Class A notes that Nature Coast Re is offering come with an initial attachment probability of 3.18%, an initial base expected loss of 1.66% and are being offered to investors with price guidance in a range for a spread of between 6.75% to 7.5%, sources said. We understand the $300 million attachment point in each case is after various inuring reinsurance arrangements and we are told an effective first-event attachment equivalent would be at around $600 million for the A notes and $1.6 billion for the AA’s. It’s important to note though, that as stated reinsurance was eroded the effective attachment could reduce in each case, we suspect. For a comparison on pricing, the Nature Coast Re 2026-1 cat bond notes issued in February came with an initial expected loss of 1.74% and priced to pay investors a spread of 8% . As you’d expect, the spreads look lower from the start with this new catastrophe bond from SafePoint, given reinsurance market pricing has continued to soften through this year. You can read all about this new Nature Coast Re Ltd. (Series 2026-2) catastrophe bond from SafePoint as well as details on almost every cat bond issued in the extensive Artemis Deal Directory . items.extracted_text: Ohio AG Sues Home-Improvement Companies for Allegedly Scamming Customers Article 0 Comments Ohio Attorney General Andy Wilson this week filed separate lawsuits against two home-improvement companies that allegedly took down payments from consumers but failed to provide the services promised or performed subpar work. One lawsuit seeks to help nine consumers who reported paying a combined $140,000 to Journey Home Restoration in Lorain County the other involves five consumers who reported more than $60,000 in combined losses to The Metal Roof Company in central Ohio. The state’s lawsuit against Journey Home Restoration and its owner, Jason Kaczur, alleges that the company accepted the $140,000 from the nine customers for roofing, siding and gutter projects that were not completed. It was filed in Lorain County Common Pleas Court. The other lawsuit against The Metal Roofing Company and its owner, Danile Toland, maintains that the company performed substandard and defective roofing work for some consumers and failed to respond when consumers reported problems with their roofs. In one case, the company allegedly accepted payment for a new roof but did not begin the project. The company, which sells and installs metal roofing, operates in central Ohio. The lawsuit was filed in Franklin County Common Pleas Court. The Ohio Attorney General’s Office has heard from five consumers who report combined losses of more than $60,000. Because the business appears to remain in operation, Wilson’s office is asking other consumers who may have experienced similar problems to come forward. items.rss_title: Taiwan to Fund $4 Billion Texas Complex for AI, Nvidia Partners
items.rss_description: Taiwan plans to raise billions of dollars to develop industrial parks in the US that would build a base for a comprehensive supply chain for Nvidia Corp. and other AI hardware makers in the country. The initiative is starting with …
items.extracted_text: Taiwan to Fund $4 Billion Texas Complex for AI, Nvidia Partners Article 0 Comments Taiwan plans to raise billions of dollars to develop industrial parks in the US that would build a base for a comprehensive supply chain for Nvidia Corp. and other AI hardware makers in the country. The initiative is starting with a complex in Texas that would cost as much as $4 billion to build, according to Taiwan’s Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin. The facilities would help smaller suppliers that are essential to the operations of Nvidia’s main production partner Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. and AI server assemblers including Foxconn Technology Group to set up shop in the US, Kung said. Each complex would run between $2 billion and $4 billion to build, and the government is planning “more than one” site on US soil, Kung said in an Oct. 12 interview with Bloomberg News. The Taiwanese government is partnering with the Taiwan Electrical and Electronic Manufacturers’ Association , which will be responsible for raising required funding to develop the complexes, he said. “We are going to establish a long-term, sustainable supply chain there that can also be joined by American firms and local workers, and not just Taiwanese companies,” Kung said. Companies like TSMC, Foxconn and Wistron Corp. provide essential hardware for data centers and are critical to the success of US AI chipmakers including Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices Inc., and cloud service providers such as Meta Platforms Inc. and Microsoft Corp. These Taiwanese manufacturing titans depend in turn on lesser-known partners that make a wide range of parts from chip packaging substrates to cooling modules — everything that’s required in an AI data center. Read More: TSMC Mulls Multibillion-Dollar Texas Site for More AI Chips But while TSMC and Foxconn are capable of funding and managing their own US expansion, that’s not always the case for smaller firms. That’s how Taiwan is hoping the new industrial complexes in the US could help. Many of these suppliers got a boost from Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang when he cited the names of a few dozen parts makers during a keynote presentation in Taipei earlier this year, a gesture that signaled how indispensable the firms are to the global AI ecosystem. Taiwanese officials will back suppliers that seek to operate in these parks, including by offering loan guarantees and helping communicate with local and federal officials in the US on needs ranging from visas to land, Kung said. Earlier this year, Taiwan pledged to help support $250 billion in credit guarantees for further investment in the American semiconductor supply chain as part of its trade deal with the US. Taiwan has already secured a plot of land for an industrial park in Texas, according to a person familiar with the matter. In response, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said it will elaborate on the plan at a suitable time. Developing a robust supply-chain on US soil has taken on new urgency for Taiwan, which is under pressure to deliver on its investment commitments under the trade deal forged with the Trump administration earlier this year. The self-governing island is also seeking to mitigate the geopolitical risks to its biggest tech manufacturers from long-standing tensions with China. Read More: TSMC’s Upbeat Outlook Fails to Quash AI Buildout Concerns TSMC alone has pledged to spend $265 billion to build advanced chipmaking plants in Arizona, the largest-ever foreign investment in America. Meanwhile, Nvidia’s major server assembly partners including Foxconn and Wistron have been expanding their US production capacity to capture growth opportunities from the domestic AI infrastructure buildout. AI demand is so massive that it’s offering a great opportunity for manufacturers to reshore production to the US, the minister said. Lucrative margins from such business can help cover the high costs initially incurred when building factories in the US, he added, and costs will gradually fall as companies scale up their operations. At the same time, Taiwanese suppliers are under huge time pressure to fulfill AI orders and are ramping up production both at home and overseas, Kung added. He said that while TSMC is making a major commitment in the US, it’s going to build “many, many more” plants at home. The Taiwanese government isn’t worried about TSMC’s global expansion, which is a move to turn its customers into strategic partners, Kung said. Read: TSMC Open to Working With Terafab But Must Control Plants Texas has become a popular destination for Taiwanese companies after both Foxconn and Wistron recently expanded their presence there. TSMC said on Thursday it’s also exploring Texas as a new site in the US, although when asked whether the company has decided on the Lone Star state, Kung said the chipmaker is looking at “many locations” for additional investments without elaborating. TSMC declined to comment. Kung quipped that Tesla Inc. CEO Elon Musk, who has vowed to take on TSMC in chipmaking, is welcome to use the new supply chain created by Taiwanese companies in the US, “though we will not completely transfer our technology to him.” Copyright 2026 Bloomberg. items.extracted_text: Adjuster Created Law Firm and Fake Claim to Defraud Insurer of $1M, Officials Charge Article 0 Comments A former claims adjuster has been charged with defrauding the Pennsylvania insurer he worked for by taking payment of nearly $1 million for an accident claim under the guise that he was with a law firm representing the claimant. Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday announced felony charges against Glenn Allen Johnson and his business, Elite Injury Representatives, LLC, alleging insurance fraud, theft by deception, forgery and other charges. Investigators maintain that Johnson, of Indiana, was employed as a claims adjuster by Donegal Insurance when he steered payment of $949,639 from Donegal to Elite Injury Representatives. According to investigators, Johnson, while employed at Donegal in 2024 and 2025, created and opened Elite Injury Representatives, which appeared to be a law firm, and utilized his position as a claims adjuster to input fraudulent documentation into the Donegal claims file. This documentation included fraudulent medical records and notes of conversations between the alleged injured party and Johnson, according to prosecutors. Based on the medical records within the file and a subsequent demand letter, also believed to be authored by Johnson, Donegal issued a payment to Elite Injury Representatives in the amount of $949, 639.54. According to officials, Johnson was arrested last week in Indiana and is awaiting extradition to Pennsylvania to face the charges. Criminal charges are merely allegations and Johnson is presumed innocent until and unless proven guilty. Was this article valuable? Yes No Here are more articles you may enjoy. items.extracted_text: The decision, in Philadelphia Indemnity Insurance Company v. Oldfields School Inc. , was issued Thursday in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland in Baltimore. In a 2025 lawsuit, a woman identified as Jane Doe alleged a teacher sexually harassed and abused her from 2005 — when she was 14 — through 2009, after she left school. The teacher was fired from the school in 2007 due to the abuse, and the student graduated in the summer of 2008, according to the ruling. The student says she still suffers from panic attacks and anxiety, has felt suicidal and requires therapy. Philadelphia, a unit of Tokio Marine, insured Oldfields under a policy running from August 2008 to August 2009, that included coverage for liability tied to sexual or physical abuse. The insurer argued that the first abuse in 2005 predated the policy and that the teacher and student had both left the school before the policy began. The judge disagreed. He said the coverage form applies when “bodily injury,” defined to include emotional distress, occurs during the policy period. Coverage, he wrote, “does not turn on the timing of the ‘abusive conduct,’” but on the timing of the bodily injury. The student alleges distress and treatment beginning in 2008, he noted, which could fall within the policy period. The judge granted the school’s cross-motion on the duty to defend but delayed a decision on whether the insurer must pay any eventual judgment until the lawsuit is resolved. items.original_title: Cal/OSHA proposes $212,500 in fines over fatal tunnel collapse
items.rss_title: Cal/OSHA proposes $212,500 in fines over fatal tunnel collapse
items.rss_description: Two California contractors face $212,500 in proposed penalties after a tunnel collapse that killed one worker and seriously injured another, the California Division of Occupational Safety and Health said Thursday.
items.extracted_text: The agency said the employers failed to provide adequate ground support at the Canyon Tunnel construction project near Knights Ferry, California, where an April 14 collapse about 200 feet inside the tunnel trapped two workers. Twyla Capurro, a 35-year-old geologist, was killed in the incident. Antioch-based Drill Tech Drilling & Shoring, which was constructing the irrigation water diversion tunnel, faces $95,000 in proposed penalties for one serious accident-related ground control violation and one “willful-serious” accident-related tunnel support violation. Clovis-based Provost & Pritchard Engineering Group, which designed the tunnel, faces $117,500 in proposed penalties for similar violations and an additional “serious” training violation. Investigators found both employers allowed work to proceed without removing or adequately supporting identified dangerous ground, according to Cal/OSHA. The more than 12,000-foot-long tunnel was being built for the South San Joaquin Irrigation District. Cal/OSHA issued the citations Sept. 30. Provost & Pritchard has appealed, the agency said. Cal/OSHA’s Bureau of Investigations is conducting a separate investigation.
